title: Saturation bleedthrough field notes
quick_findings: Observed persistent tail latency amplification on otherwise healthy nodes when neighbor pool reached steady saturation ("bleedthrough")
KV cache priming and prefix cache eviction patterns correlate strongly with bleedthrough episodes
Small adjustments to auto-batching timeout reduce p99 in short bursts but increase median under sustained QPS
Network egress queueing on proxy layer contributed ~6–12ms to p99 during peak bleedthrough windows
numeric_summary: Baseline (no saturation): p50=12ms p95=28ms p99=46ms throughput=480 qps/node (seq=128)
Saturation window: p50=15ms p95=68ms p99=210ms throughput=480 qps/node (same config)
Mitigation candidate A (batch-timeout -10ms): p50=14ms p95=52ms p99=92ms, median cost -3%
Mitigation candidate B (force-prefill=on): p50=13ms p95=33ms p99=54ms, 10% extra memory used, throughput steady
Observed network egress contribution to p99 during bleedthrough: +6–12ms (tcp retransmissions rare, queueing dominant)
experiments_run: exp-2024-11-16-a: zipfian arrivals (theta=0.9), 480 qps/node, seq=128, model=rw-7b-compat, quant=fp16, batch_timeout=40ms
exp-2024-11-17-b: same load, batch_timeout=30ms, prefill disabled
exp-2024-11-21-d: introduced proxy egress shaping (burst=100ms, limit=1Gbps) to reproduce queueing
exp-2024-11-25-e: synthetic neighbor-saturation: staggered one node to 100% utilization to observe cross-node effects
config_snippets: node profile: 8xA10G, 96GB RAM, kernel: 6.2, nic: mellanox-25g
proxy: envoy v1.27 with upstream buffer limits: max_request_bytes=65536, per_host_connections=16
body:
High-level goal: understand an intermittent pattern where p99 jumps to 3–4x baseline even though node-level CPU/GPU utilization looks normal. We hypothesize a 'bleedthrough' phenomenon: when a subset of the pool saturates (either due to a cold-cache neighborhood or misrouted burst), other nodes in the pool experience elevated tail latency due to shared resources (proxy queues, prefix cache churn, and request coalescing mismatches).

Notes from preliminary runs:
- Repro recipe: run 480 qps/node with zipfian client (theta ~0.9) and a mix of short (seq=64) and medium (seq=128) prompts. We see the bleedthrough window after ~45–90s of sustained load.
- Symptom timeline: median rises slightly first (+10–20%), then p95 jumps, then p99 spikes hard (>150ms), then slowly decays as caches re-prime or the pool rebalances. Not tied to OOMs or GPU throttling.
- Telemetry correlations: increased KV-cache evictions, elevated upstream retransmit counts, and longer wait times on proxy worker threads.

Interesting observations per run:
- exp-a (baseline): clean tail, occasional small spikes; KV-hit-rate ~72% stable.
- exp-b (shorter batch-timeout): p99 improves relative to exp-a during spikes but p50/p95 slightly worse during steady state. Lowering batch timeout reduces coalescing benefits and increases per-request overhead.
- exp-c (force-prefill): big reduction in p99 spikes; KV-hit-rate jumps to ~88%. Memory footprint up ~10%. This suggests prefix priming is a major lever.
- exp-d (proxy shaping): able to reproduce >50% of p99 delta by adding a small egress queue; shows network queuing is a real contributor, likely amplifying small scheduling mismatches.
- exp-e (neighbor saturation): deliberately push one node to saturation by introducing heavy context sequences; neighboring nodes see ~2–3x increase in p99 with minimal CPU/GPU load increase. This is the classic bleedthrough signature.

Hypothesis and mechanism (working):
1) A saturated node (hot shard of contexts or a misrouted burst) causes upstream proxy queues to back up; envoy upstream buffers start queuing and per-host connection pools are exhausted.
2) Some requests are auto-routed to other nodes but arrive with partially primed caches/kv state leading to extra kernel work (prefill, kv warmup) and longer processing times.
3) Auto-batching/coalescing logic expecting certain arrival patterns breaks under these cross-node shifts; larger batches occasionally form but complete slower, stretching tails.
4) Network queueing and small TCP queueing amplify the effective tail.

Preliminary mitigation candidates tried:
- Force-prefill / prewarm prefixes for heavy context classes (worked well but memory cost).
- Slightly reduce batch_timeout to favor latency in short bursts (reduces p99 for bursts but hurts throughput efficiency).
- Adjust proxy upstream buffer policy (smaller buffers + early backpressure) to fail fast rather than queueing long. This shows promise in reducing amplified tails.
- Preferential routing: avoid routing new requests to nodes that have seen >X% prefill/eviction churn in last T seconds (needs routing signals).

Notes on instrumentation improvements needed:
- Add kv-cache timeline traces to request-level spans (timestamp evictions and warms).
- Surface per-host envoy queue occupancy metric into our per-request trace sampling to correlate queue depth with p99.
conclusions: Bleedthrough is a multi-factor effect: prefix cache churn + proxy queueing + batching mismatch. No single fix will eliminate it.
Force-prefill is the most effective single mitigation observed but costs memory; good for dedicated pools or tiered SLA customers.
Proxy-level shaping/backpressure to avoid head-of-line queueing is low-cost and reduces p99 amplification significantly.
Batch timeout tuning is a tradeoff: lower gives better burst p99, higher gives better steady-state throughput.
next_steps: Implement per-request kv-cache span (instrumentation), sample 1% of requests during next run
Prototype a routing flag: 'recent-eviction-score' propagated by nodes; route away if >0.6
Run longer neighbor-saturation experiments (10–20m) to test steady-state behavior and rollback windows
Discuss dedicated-prefill toggle as a product config for Dedicated customers (CS/PRD note)
Follow-up with infra to surface envoy per-host queue depth to telemetry (ticket created Jira-5779)
